description: Class, sequence, activity, and state diagrams.

screens.body:
UML — the Unified Modeling Language — is a shared visual vocabulary for software design. Instead of describing your design in paragraphs, you draw it in diagrams every developer can read.

Drawing first is cheap; coding first is expensive. A diagram exposes a bad design in minutes, while the same mistake in code costs days of rewriting.

options: A shared visual vocabulary for software design
check.question: UML is…

screens.heading: Why draw before coding
screens.keyPoint: Diagrams expose bad designs while they're still cheap to fix.

screens.body:
A class diagram shows the system's structure. Each class is a box with three compartments: the name on top, attributes (data it holds) in the middle, methods (things it does) at the bottom.

A + means public, a − means private. You don't model every class — you model the important ones and their relationships, enough to see the shape of the system.
screens.heading: Class diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Boxes of name, attributes, methods — the system's skeleton.

screens.body:
Classes relate in a few key ways. Association is a plain connection: a Student enrolls in a Course. Inheritance is an is-a: a Manager is an Employee (hollow arrow pointing at the parent).

Composition is a strong has-a: a House owns its Rooms — destroy the house, the rooms go too (filled diamond). Aggregation is a weaker has-a: a Team has Players, but players survive the team folding.

check.question: A Manager is an Employee. That's…

screens.heading: Relationships

screens.body:
A sequence diagram shows one scenario playing out over time. Time flows downward. Each participant gets a vertical lifeline; horizontal arrows are messages sent between them; the thin bars (activations) show when an object is busy.

Read it like a script: Customer → Website: login(), Website → Database: findUser(). It's the best diagram for 'what talks to what, in which order.'

code.snippet:
Customer -> Website: login(name, pw)
Website -> Database: findUser(name)
Database --> Website: user record
Website --> Customer: "welcome back"
// read top to bottom: who calls whom, in order

screens.heading: Sequence diagrams
screens.keyPoint: One scenario, top to bottom: who calls whom.

screens.body:
An activity diagram is a flowchart for behavior: rounded boxes for actions, diamonds for decisions, thick bars for fork/join where work splits into parallel paths and merges back.

Use it for workflows and business processes: 'order placed → payment verified → if approved, ship; if declined, notify.' When the logic has branches and parallel steps, this diagram keeps it honest.

options: Workflows with decisions and parallel steps
check.question: Activity diagrams are best for…

screens.heading: Activity diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Flowcharts for behavior: actions, decisions, forks.

screens.body:
A state machine diagram shows one object's lifecycle: rounded boxes are states, arrows are transitions labeled with the event that triggers them. An Order goes New → Paid → Shipped → Delivered.

Use it when an object has meaningful states and rules about moving between them — orders, accounts, game characters. It answers 'what can happen to this thing, and when?'

options: States and the events that move between them
check.question: A state machine diagram shows…

screens.heading: State machine diagrams
screens.keyPoint: One object's lifecycle: states, events, transitions.

screens.body:
Pick by question. 'What's the structure?' → class diagram. 'What calls what, in which order?' → sequence diagram. 'How does this workflow branch?' → activity diagram. 'What states can this thing be in?' → state machine.

You rarely need all four for every feature. One right diagram beats four decorative ones.

options: Pick the diagram that answers your question
check.question: The rule for choosing a UML diagram is…

screens.heading: Which diagram when
screens.keyPoint: Match the diagram to the question you're asking.

screens.body: UML specification and reference — uml.org (Object Management Group). PlantUML for drawing diagrams as text — plantuml.com.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: The UML spec is the authority; PlantUML makes drawing fast.
